stem: When does a session (or batch) actually start — that is, when does its maximum TTL timer begin counting?

options.text: When its first job begins running.
The moment you construct the `Session`/`Batch` object.
When you exit the context manager block.
When you submit the first job, whether or not it has started running.
When the session's interactive TTL first elapses.

explanation.correct: A session or batch starts when its first job begins execution; that is when the maximum TTL timer starts. (Note: if you open a session but submit no jobs for 30 minutes, it closes automatically.)

distractors.B: Merely constructing the object does not start the clock — the first job entering execution does.
distractors.C: Exiting the context manager closes the session/batch; it does not start the TTL timer.
distractors.D: Creating the service only authenticates you; it is unrelated to when a session's timer begins.
distractors.E: Submission is not the trigger — the clock starts when that first job actually begins executing. A job that sits in the queue for an hour does not eat into the maximum TTL.
distractors.F: The interactive TTL measures the idle gap between jobs and only ever ends a session early; it has nothing to do with starting the maximum TTL clock.

provenance.notes: meta-pattern fix pass: length/stem-echo/absolute calibration (s4) — made the correct option the shortest (shortest-option calibration). Also: de-code-formatted a distractor (format-tell fix). | pool wave: +E (submission starts the clock), +F (the interactive TTL starts it)
